## Build v96 (2026-10-29): Engine-calendar fix F2 — the work-year refundable education credit deposits the following spring, matching the plan march

All user-entered data, no external source; no schema, UI, or credit-computation change (the credit computation itself is untouched). Group 2 of the engine-calendar fix program (finding F2, from the settled round-13 audit): the work-years pricer added the refundable portion of the year's education credit to the same year's surplus, so it banked into Taxable at that year's end — cash the household had not yet received, available a year early to fund that year's deficit settlement — and the in-code comment claimed parity with the retirement march on timing. The march does the opposite: it carries the refundable portion undeposited as a pending amount and lands it in the taxable pool at the start of the next simulated year, at full basis, before that year's yields, growth, and settlement run, so it funds the following year and grows with the pool; a credit earned in the plan's final year, which has no following year inside the plan, is instead added to the ending taxable balance after the final year's growth, as the undeposited dollars themselves. CORRECTION — the work-years roll follows the march's carry/deposit shape rather than inventing a new one. The same-year surplus now excludes the refundable portion entirely (the nonrefundable portion keeps reducing the same year's tax through the shared pricer, unchanged), the one-year pricer reports the refundable portion on its line so the roll can carry it, and the roll deposits the pending amount at the start of the next simulated year, before that year's yields, growth, and settlement, through the existing ledger landing at full basis — so the deposit funds the next year's spending and taxes, earns that year's yield, and grows with the pool, exactly as the march's deposit does, and a deficit year can no longer fund itself from cash that arrives the next spring. HORIZON-END HANDLING (decided explicitly): a refundable credit arising in the roll's last work year is added to the quit-age taxable balance after the loop, after the final year's growth, at full basis, flowing into the rolled plan's opening taxable balance and rebuilt basis fields so the retirement march prices on it from its first year — never dropped, and never deposited twice, since the loop's deposit block already consumed every earlier year's credit at the next year's start. ZERO-YEAR PATH (checked): no work year is priced, so no work-year refund arises and nothing is threaded into the march; the rolled inputs are unchanged and the march prices education credits for its own years through its own pending-refund carry. TOTALS: refund deposits that actually land in Taxable — start-of-year deposits plus the horizon-end deposit — count into the roll's surplus-banked total, so the totals still name every dollar the surplus-and-refund stream landed. The published contract prose is corrected with the same change: the education-credit semantics clause now states the next-spring timing for work years instead of the same-year banking it previously described. REGRESSION FIXTURE: a new tax fixture named for the mechanism pins the re-derived example — a work-years case producing the full credit on the qualifying expense, with its refundable portion reported on the year's line: the same-year surplus differs from the no-student control by exactly the nonrefundable portion, and the next simulated year's opening taxable pool includes the deposit, proven by the yield gap on that year's opening balance after removing the yield on the surplus gap, together with a one-year horizon-end leg proving the last year's credit still lands in the quit-age balance at full basis. FIXTURE RE-DERIVATION FOUND IN REVIEW: one standing fixture pinned the defective behaviour itself — its same-year surplus expectations included the refundable portion — so its surplus expectations were re-derived under the corrected timing, with the earlier derivation preserved in its note as history; its roll taxable figures are unchanged, because its credit arises in its only work year and the horizon-end deposit lands the same dollars. ACCEPTANCE: three consecutive clean internal review passes; typechecks for both bundles; the tax census in fine slices totalling every fixture in the suite (one slice of the six-chunk run was killed for memory and re-run in finer slices, each with its teeth check passing); the extended, December, UI-state, Roth CAS, retirement CAS, and retirement suites green with the integrity checks at zero violations; the packaged harness green across its census and its main-process checks; and the stored-record anchors reproduced bit-identically on all four anchor figures, confirming the plan march did not move. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures (figures live in fixtures, described qualitatively in prose). API_CONTRACT_VERSION 95 → 96.

## Build v95 (2026-10-29): Engine-calendar fix F1 — the applicable-percentage table keys on the real coverage year, decoupled from the guideline-row relabel

All user-entered data, no external source; no schema, UI, or new law-table change. Group 1 of the engine-calendar fix program (finding F1, from the settled round-13 audit): the single-year pricer carries one coverage-year value that served two purposes. Under the projection's newest convention the pricer relabels the earliest coverage year to the year after the newest guideline row, so the statutory lookback inside the premium-credit function lands on the newest guideline row and the cliff prices off that row, in today's dollars — the sanctioned plan convention. But the same relabelled value also selected the applicable-percentage table, so the relabelled year priced on the following year's published table instead of its own year's table, and the Playground diverged from the plan march, which prices that same economic year on its own year's table. Only the table followed the relabel: the guideline row, the cliff, and the benchmark handling were already correct, and the defect is specific to the relabelled year. CORRECTION — split the threading. The premium-credit function takes a new optional table year: absent, it defaults to the coverage year, so every existing caller prices exactly as before; when supplied, it governs only the table lookup, while the coverage year keeps governing the guideline-row lookback, the cliff, and the cliff's start year. The single-year pricer is the one split caller: it keeps passing the relabelled year as the coverage year (the guideline row is unchanged) and passes the real coverage year as the table year, at both of its premium-credit calls — the main ACA block and the without-gains comparison that feeds the gains flags. No new table is added, no guideline row changes, and no other surface is touched: the plan march passes no table year and keeps its own behaviour, the December console never selects the newest convention, and the published contract text describing the following year's table scope already states the rule in terms of the real coverage year and needs no change. UNAFFECTED CASES: the relabel is the identity for the following year, so that year keeps its own table; later years still fall back to the earliest complete table; the statutory lookback convention is untouched; and pre-earliest years keep the real year with no cliff invented. The convention comments at the pricer now state the split rule where they previously stated that the table follows the relabelled value. REGRESSION FIXTURE: a new tax fixture named for the mechanism pins the re-derived example through the single-year pricer under the newest convention — the credit under the real year's table with the guideline row pinned to the newest row — together with the unaffected cases bit-identically (the following year, a later year, the lookback convention, and a pre-earliest year). FIXTURE RE-DERIVATION FOUND IN REVIEW: one standing projection fixture pinned the defective behaviour itself — its projected credit for the relabelled year was derived from the following year's table — so its expected projected credit and its note were re-derived under the corrected table selection, with the earlier derivation preserved in the note as history; every other field in that fixture is unchanged, and it is the only standing fixture that moved. ACCEPTANCE: three consecutive clean internal review passes; typechecks for both bundles; the tax census in fine slices (one slice needed splitting further after an out-of-memory kill, and every slice then passed with its teeth check); the extended, December, UI-state, Roth CAS, retirement CAS, and retirement suites green with the integrity checks at zero violations; the packaged harness green across its census and its main-process checks; and the stored-record anchors — the compare run from the stored record with no scenario overrides — reproduced bit-identically on all four anchor figures, confirming the plan march did not move. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 94 → 95.

## Build v94 (2026-10-29): Stored-data fix F6 — restore preflight validates the legacy bucket field so an accepted restore cannot poison a later export

All user-entered data, no external source; no engine, pricing, schema, or UI change. Group 5 (final group) of the stored-data fix program (finding F6, MEDIUM, SHOULD-FIX): the backup schema typed the Net Worth account bucket as an unrestricted string with no preflight bucket validation, the restore stored it verbatim, and the export path runs decryptStr on it whenever it carries the reserved prefix — so a restore carrying a malformed prefixed bucket was accepted and every later export threw, refusing all exports until the dataset was repaired another way. BUCKET-DOMAIN DETERMINATION (evidence, from code and history): no current writer sets the bucket — the account add/rename handlers and the Net Worth seed builder all omit it, so live rows carry the database default, and the only writers that ever produce a bucket value are the database default and the restore itself; no writer in the repository history encrypts it, and the only read path decrypting it is the export path, which reads it leniently (plaintext returns as itself, prefixed values decrypt under the bucket field context with the dual-read: the field-bound form first, the legacy no-associated-data form second). The export comment records that older rows hold encrypted values, and the encryption-at-rest era is the only mechanism that could have produced them, so a genuinely decryptable prefixed value is a legitimate legacy form that must keep restoring. The legitimate domain is therefore exactly what the export reader accepts: any plaintext value, plus any prefixed value that decrypts in the bucket field context. No narrower plaintext domain is enforced — no writer restricts which plaintext tag a legacy row may carry, and inventing one could refuse valid legacy backups. PREFLIGHT RULE: before any write, a bucket value carrying the reserved prefix is refused unless the caller's decrypt verdict says it genuinely decrypts under the current key in the bucket field's own context; the refusal names the bucket field and the value class, and the prior dataset stays untouched. The handler computes the verdict with a real decrypt attempt in exactly the export path's context — the same context literal at both sites, verified to agree, no second context invented — following the existing pattern of injecting crypto verdicts into the pure preflight (as with the key-check verdict and the MAC verdict). A prefixed bucket with no verifier supplied is refused (fail closed). Valid values keep storing verbatim, as before: plaintext exports as itself and genuine ciphertext exports through the same dual-read, so no stored bytes change shape. The unauthenticated-legacy MAC rule is untouched (only a mismatching MAC refuses; an absent MAC still restores labelled unauthenticated). SIBLING SCAN (every field the export path decrypts, and every verbatim-stored field a later operation decrypts): (1) the eleven encrypted-at-rest settings — already guarded, cleared as fixed before this group: the restore decrypt-verifies a prefixed value in its destination context and re-encrypts it, never storing it verbatim, and encrypts plaintext values on store (harness section P proves a transplanted ciphertext restore is refused with state untouched); (2) every row text and amount field — cleared: the export carries decrypted values, the restore re-encrypts each through the reserved-prefix guard, which refuses an undecryptable prefixed value before the replacement batch, and amounts are schema-typed numbers that cannot carry a prefix at all, so no poisoned value in these fields can be accepted; (3) the typed settings — cleared: the target and reserve-start-month validations refuse any prefixed value outright, and the opening reserve's plaintext path refuses non-integer values while its prefixed form takes the decrypt-verification path; (4) every remaining settings key — cleared: the plain-text readers compare values or parse leniently with a fallback, never decrypt, so a prefixed value degrades leniently and cannot throw on a later load, and the one key whose reader does decrypt a prefixed value (the Net Worth target) is covered by (3); the restore-epoch key's carried value is dropped and recomputed in any case; (5) structural fields (enums, dates, months, flags, ids, server-assigned values) — cleared: preflight enum, date, flag, and id checks govern them and no later operation decrypts them. No sibling shares the defect, so no sibling needed a new rule; the bucket is the only field stored verbatim while its export reader decrypts. PATHS CHECKED: the hosted restorebackup action is the only hosted restore entry (the client has no direct caller); the packaged runtime dispatches the same action module over the same payload, and its portable-backup import calls restorebackup after unwrapping the file envelope, so the same preflight covers hosted and packaged with no packaged-only code; the seed builders, statement imports, and file-listing/deletion handlers never restore rows and never set the bucket, and no other entry point bypasses preflight. ACCEPTANCE is proven by two new extended fixtures (an undecryptable prefixed bucket refused at preflight in two value classes with the prior state byte-identical and the reason naming the bucket, and the valid legacy forms — plaintext, model ciphertext standing in for genuine ciphertext, and an unrestricted plaintext tag — restoring with values landing verbatim) and by packaged harness section S (real actions on throwaway stores with real encryption): the poisoned value refused with the prior total intact and exports still working, a plaintext bucket restoring and exporting again, a legacy no-associated-data ciphertext bucket and a field-bound ciphertext bucket each restoring and exporting to their plaintext tags, and a second undecryptable value class refusing the same way. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 93 → 94.

## Build v93 (2026-10-29): Stored-data fix F5 — a restore epoch so a stale editor cannot overwrite restored snapshots

All user-entered data, no external source; no engine, pricing, or schema change. Group 4 of the stored-data fix program (finding F5, MEDIUM, SHOULD-FIX): a backup restore replaced the whole dataset while restored snapshots restarted at revision 0 (the backup payload carries no revision counter and the restore insert provided none), so an editor holding a pre-restore base revision equal to the restarted revision was accepted and its whole-snapshot write silently overwrote the restored balances. Merely preserving the backup's revision number would not fix it — an older preserved revision can collide with a stale editor's base the same way — so the fix is a restore generation the CAS check honors. DESIGN: one global restore epoch for the whole dataset, not a per-snapshot stamp. A restore replaces the entire dataset in one atomic batch, so a single generation counter is the exact unit that changes; per-snapshot columns would need a schema migration and a backup-payload change for no additional protection, and the existing Roth-blob stamp pattern (a per-record revision stamped on restore) was not forced onto snapshots for the same reason — the epoch is the dataset-level analogue of that stamp. STORAGE AND ADVANCE: the epoch lives in the settings table under the key nw_restore_epoch_v1, stored as a plain integer string. It is a generation counter — structural metadata like the snapshot revision column, not a financial value — so it is stored unencrypted, like the revision, and it is not added to the encrypted-at-rest settings list. Absent or unparseable reads as epoch 0, the era before any restore stamped one. restorebackup advances it on EVERY restore, in the same atomic batch as the replacement rows: one past the epoch the destination dataset was on before the restore, read from the destination's own settings rows alongside the Roth stamp read. A carried epoch value in the backup payload is never trusted — the handler drops any payload row under the epoch key and stamps the freshly computed value instead — so backups written before epochs existed, and backups carrying a stale epoch value, still advance the epoch; a second restore advances it again. A restore refused at preflight writes nothing and advances nothing. CAS CHECK: decideCasRevision in server/src/casCore.ts takes the stored epoch and the editor's observed epoch alongside the revision pair. The epoch check runs first and is independent of the revision: a supplied epoch differing from the stored epoch is refused as an epoch conflict even when the revision numbers match — the restored-snapshot collision exactly — with a distinct reason naming the restore cause, and the stored snapshot stays intact. A missing epoch keeps the pre-v93 revision-only check, the same tolerated legacy leniency as a missing baseRevision; no live editor omits it. Ordinary revision CAS is unchanged: a stale revision without any restore is refused with the ordinary newer-copy reason, and a fresh revision is accepted. ACTIONS CARRYING IT: getNetWorth publishes restoreEpoch alongside the snapshots; updateNwSnapshot and updateNwBalance accept an optional baseEpoch (the epoch the editor observed when it loaded) and enforce it as above — those are the only two snapshot edit paths that use the revision guard, and both honor the epoch. The client editors pass the epoch they observed, frozen at editor mount (the snapshot revision already travels frozen in the snapshot object; the epoch prop arrives from the live query, so reading it at save time would re-base an open editor if a refetch landed after a restore). EDITOR BEHAVIOUR: an editor whose view predates a restore is refused with the restore-naming reason on either writer; a fresh editor that reads after the restore succeeds normally with the current epoch and revision advancing as before; after a second restore, editors from the first-restore era are refused again. PATHS CHECKED (every write to the snapshot tables): addNwSnapshot creates a new snapshot no stale editor can hold, so it takes no epoch; deleteNwSnapshot removes the row, so a later save finds nothing and cannot overwrite; the seed builders write first-run rows only; the AAD migration rewrite touches only the note ciphertext of existing rows and changes no balance or guard; Net Worth CSV/OFX imports go through addNwSnapshot; and the Roth/December engines read snapshots but never write them — no other snapshot write path exists, in either runtime. Both runtimes share the one restorebackup handler (the packaged runtime dispatches the same action over the same payload, verified in the packaged sources), so the epoch covers hosted and packaged alike with no packaged-only code. This supersedes the build v65 DATA-PLAN sentence stating that a restored snapshot restarts at revision 0 with no guard: the revision still restarts, and the epoch is now the guard that makes the restart safe. ACCEPTANCE is proven by two new extended fixtures (api-cas-restore-epoch and api-cas-restore-epoch-interleaving, pinning the decision function, the epoch parse/advance helpers, the legacy-omission tolerance, and the reviewer's interleaving step by step) and by packaged harness section R (real actions on throwaway stores with real encryption): the reviewer's exact interleaving on a fixture copy (pre-restore read, restore replacing the balance with revision restarting at 0, stale write with the pre-restore revision and epoch refused with the restore-naming reason, restored balance intact, on both writers), a post-restore fresh editor succeeding with the revision advancing normally, ordinary revision CAS unchanged without a restore, and a second restore from a MAC-stripped payload carrying a stale epoch value stamping the next epoch and refusing the first-restore-era editor while a fresh editor succeeds. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 92 → 93.

## Build v92 (2026-10-29): Stored-data fix F4 — a packaged wipe purges the retained database generation

All user-entered data, no external source; no engine, pricing, or UI change. Group 3 of the stored-data fix program (finding F4, HIGH, SHOULD-FIX): in the packaged build, a successful clearAllData persisted the empty image as a new generation while the generation protocol retained the previous generation as its fallback copy, so the full pre-wipe database image stayed readable in the same store under its generation chunk keys. MECHANISM: the wipe signal is threaded from clearAllData through the packaged runtime dispatch into the persist/cleanup path as a flag on the persist call. The dispatch sets the flag only when the action is clearAllData, the handler ran, the response validated, and the response carries ok true; a refused wipe, a handler throw, and a response-validation failure all leave the flag unset, so a failed or refused wipe never purges the fallback or any data a failed wipe left behind. persist() with the flag set runs its ordinary write-verify-pointer-switch sequence unchanged, then its cleanup removes EVERY prior generation, including the retained gen − 1 fallback, instead of only generations older than gen − 1. The just-committed generation is never removed: after a wipe it is the empty image and the store's state, so the store stays usable and a fresh write/read cycle works on top of it. The purge runs only after the pointer switch, so a failure anywhere earlier (quota, verification, stale tab) leaves the prior generations intact exactly as for any persist. SCOPE LIMIT (binding): generations only. The purge deletes generation chunk keys and nothing else: the at-rest encryption key, the backup vault, and the RSA key pair remain in the store after a wipe, exactly as before, and the wipe is not presented as complete erasure beyond generations. OPEN DECISION — key/vault retention: what remains after a wipe is the key that decrypts every stored value, the vault backups that hold full dataset images, and the RSA keys that unwrap them, all in the same origin as the wiped data. A future ruling must decide whether a wipe should also remove or rotate the key material and vault backups (and, if so, what happens to a later reload, to portable backups already exported, and to the seeded-flag behaviour that currently survives a wipe), or whether retaining them stays the documented behaviour; this group deliberately decides none of it. ORDINARY PERSISTS UNCHANGED: retention of gen − 1 stays exactly as-is for every non-wipe persist, including the boot commit in initLocalDb, which never follows a wipe. PATHS CHECKED: the runtime dispatch persist-after-action is the only persist after an action in the packaged runtime; initLocalDb's boot persist, the first-run seed dispatch (an ordinary dispatch), the portable backup export/import dispatches (exportbackup and restorebackup — a restore after a wipe retains only the empty wipe image as its fallback), the probe's export/clear/restore sequence, and the persist-on-failure path (which runs the same flagged persist call, so a successful wipe whose persist then fails on a non-stale reason still purges only after its pointer switch, and a failed wipe keeps its fallback) all go through the flagged call or a plain call as their outcome requires; no other persist call exists in the packaged sources, and the hosted build has no generation protocol, so clearAllData there needs no change. ACCEPTANCE is proven in the packaged harness (new section Q, real actions on throwaway stores with real encryption): a store at generation 5 wiped through the real dispatch leaves no chunk key for any prior generation (fallback and planted stale older chunks included), commits the empty image as the next generation, keeps the encryption key, reloads empty and usable, and reads back a fresh write after reload; an ordinary persist retains exactly its gen − 1 fallback and advances the pointer; and a refused wipe keeps its fallback and its data. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 91 → 92.

## Build v91 (2026-10-29): Stored-data fix F1 — ciphertext is bound to its field via AES-GCM associated data

All user-entered data, no external source; no engine, pricing, or UI change. Group 2 of the stored-data fix program (finding F1, HIGH, SHOULD-FIX): field encryption used one AES-GCM key with no associated data, so a valid ciphertext transplanted into another field, row, or column decrypted silently to the source value. Every encrypt and decrypt call site now carries a field-binding context, used as AES-GCM additionalData on both sides. AAD CONSTRUCTION: the associated data is the UTF-8 encoding of "fp-aad-v1:" + the context string, where the context is "table.column" for row values (the database's own table and column names, as string literals at each call site — e.g. the yearly-expense amount and the monthly-summary amount are different contexts) and "settings:<key>" for settings values (via settingContext, including the encryption key-check value, the opening reserve, the retirement and Roth planner blobs, the December and Roth/Playground UI-state blobs, both import-settings blobs, both sticky entry defaults, and the Net Worth target). The "fp-aad-v1:" namespace means a future scheme revision can never collide with this binding. STABILITY ARGUMENT: record identity is deliberately not bound. Encryption happens before the row exists (seed, import, restore, and every insert encrypt before the database assigns an id), and legitimate flows move a plaintext value between rows (a version row's amount is denormalised into its parent bill row; restore re-encrypts every value into freshly inserted rows), while field identity is stable across all of those flows. The residual a database writer keeps is a transplant within the SAME column across rows, which no pre-insert scheme can bind; cross-field transplants, the reviewer's reproduction, are refused with the generic undecryptable error, never a silently wrong value. MIGRATION: dual-read. Reads try the bound form first and fall back to the legacy no-AAD form, so every pre-v91 ciphertext keeps reading; plaintext (non-prefixed) values read as before. Re-encryption with the binding happens (a) on every write — every writer re-encrypts the whole row or blob it touches, under the destination contexts; (b) on first load after the upgrade for table rows, the opening reserve, both import-settings blobs, and the key-check value — the loaders' existing compare-and-write / in-place migration writes (build v64, A4) now also trigger on legacy ciphertext via needsRebind, so the rewrite is idempotent and a concurrent newer write still wins; and (c) on restore, which decrypts and re-encrypts every value. RESIDUAL WINDOW: a legacy ciphertext stays transplantable only until its row is first loaded (table rows, opening reserve, import settings, key-check — in practice the first dashboard or Net Worth load after the upgrade), or until its blob is next saved or the dataset is restored (settings blobs, whose getters stay read-only: the retirement, Roth, December, and UI-state blobs upgrade on next save, never on read, so read paths and revision/CAS predicates never rewrite bytes). A legacy ciphertext in a store that is never loaded and never saved keeps the window until one of those events; the fallback accepts only ciphertext produced under the same install key, and every new-scheme ciphertext is immune from the first write. Dropping the legacy branch is a future contract's decision, once live stores have all passed through a load or save under this build. SITES UPDATED: the encryptStr / decryptStr / decryptNum / encryptNum / decryptNullable / encryptNullable primitives (context is a required parameter, so no call site can compile without one), the encPrefixCore reserved-prefix verifier inside encryptStr (strict bound-form verify for passthrough; a legacy ciphertext for the field is decrypted and re-encrypted with the binding instead of passing through; a ciphertext bound to another field is refused like typed text), ensureKeyCheck, decryptSettingValue and readStoredBlob (both take the settings key), every row loader and writer in the spending and Net Worth families, the seed builders, the backup export decrypt branches (including the legacy Net Worth bucket column), the restore handler, the import batch verifier (which now tries all three transaction text-field contexts, since the preflight cannot know which field a value was bound to, and the insert writers then bind it to its actual destination), and the Roth/Retirement/December/UI-state blob handlers. VERBATIM-CIPHERTEXT-COPY PATHS FOUND AND THEIR DISPOSITIONS: (1) three creation sites reused one ciphertext variable for a parent row and its first version row — the seed smoothed bills, addYearlyExpense, and addMonthlyBill — each now encrypts the version row separately with the version column's context; (2) the restore settings loop stored a backup's ciphertext value verbatim after verifying it — it now always decrypts and re-encrypts with the destination key's context, so a transplanted ciphertext inside a backup is refused at preflight/build time with zero writes (the transplanted-ciphertext restore leg in harness section P proves this; a legacy no-AAD ciphertext in a backup restores and is re-encrypted bound); (3) the encPrefix passthrough in encryptStr — strict-verify per the destination context, per above; (4) parent-row denormalisations (latest version amount copied into the parent bill/expense row) — already decrypt-then-re-encrypt in every case, verified by audit; five of those sites had their contexts corrected in review from the version column to the parent column, which is the column they write; (5) the sticky entry defaults (paid-by labels stored under settings keys, written from the bill add/edit handlers) — bound to their settings keys, not to the bill columns the same handlers write, after review caught the script's first pass binding them to the bill columns; (6) snapshot duplication, CSV/OFX import, and seed Net Worth balances — no verbatim copies exist; every value is encrypted fresh for its destination (Net Worth balances go through nwBalanceRowValues, whose per-split helper now takes the destination context per column). No other path copies an enc:v1: value between fields, rows, or tables. ACCEPTANCE is proven in the packaged harness (new section P, real actions on throwaway stores with real encryption): a yearly-expense amount ciphertext transplanted into a monthly summary, and a monthly-bill name ciphertext transplanted into a yearly expense, are both refused on load (the read throws; no wrong figure is ever returned); every field family round-trips through its real write/read actions; a legacy no-AAD ciphertext planted in a table row reads correctly and is re-encrypted bound by the load; a legacy no-AAD ciphertext planted in a settings blob reads correctly through the dual-read; a restore of a legacy-ciphertext backup succeeds and stores bound values; a restore carrying a transplanted ciphertext is refused with state untouched; and the seeded anchors and December fixtures are unchanged. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 90 → 91.

REVIEW FIX-UP, same contract (2026-10-29): the first full harness run caught a migration defect the scripted call-site pass had introduced — every decryptSettingValue / readStoredBlob call site passed a settingContext-wrapped key while both wrappers apply settingContext themselves, so every settings-blob read decrypted under a doubled context and failed: the December guarded-update save conflicted, a dashboard load after a bill add (sticky entry defaults present) threw, and backup export of the sticky/import settings threw. All eleven read sites now pass the bare settings key (the writers were already correct), with a guard comment on both wrappers stating the bare-key convention, and the harness passes whole (285 checks: the prior 252 plus 33 new section P checks, including the December CAS and stale-tab suites that caught the defect). No design or migration-policy change: the defect never shipped, and no stored bytes were affected.

## Build v90 (2026-10-29): Stored-data fixes F2+F3 — the December projection blob and the Roth/Playground UI-state blob are encrypted at rest

All user-entered data, no external source; no engine, pricing, or UI change. Group 1 of the stored-data fix program (both findings HIGH, SHOULD-FIX): (F2) the December projection console's saved inputs (settings key december_projection_v1) and (F3) the Roth view / Playground remembered form state (settings key roth_ui_state_v1) were stored as bare plaintext JSON while every other financial value is encrypted. Both blobs are now stored as enc:v1: ciphertext under the existing app key and scheme (encryptStr, AES-256-GCM, no new crypto primitives, no new key material): the save handlers encrypt the serialized blob before it reaches settings, and the read handlers decrypt before parsing. Dual-read: a record stored before this build, in legacy plaintext JSON, reads exactly as before with zero user action — the enc:v1: prefix is the whole distinction, the same dual-read the other encrypted values already give. The pure serialize/parse and write-decision functions are untouched (they stay plaintext-JSON functions, like the Roth plan record's split/join pair; the envelope lives in the handlers), so no parsed figure can move. The Roth UI-state CAS guard changes with the envelope: the previous SQL guard read the revision out of the stored JSON with json_extract, which cannot see inside ciphertext, so the commit now predicates on the stored raw value itself via commitSettingsValueGuarded (ciphertext byte equality, the Roth plan record's pattern, sound because every encryption uses a fresh random nonce); the revision decision on the decrypted read is unchanged and its pure mirror fixtures are untouched. Export now decrypts both blobs like the other encrypted settings (so a backup restores under a different key instead of travelling as source-install ciphertext), and both keys are added to restoreCore's ENCRYPTED_AT_REST_SETTING_KEYS, so a restore re-encrypts a backup's plaintext value under the destination key (traced through the restore handler's settings loop: the list branch encrypts a non-prefixed value and decrypt-verifies a prefixed one before storing it as-is). The restore contract text and the whitelist pin fixture name both keys (pin now eleven keys, exact). No other reader or writer of either key exists: the client reads both only through the get actions, no other server core references either key, and the packaged runtime dispatches the same handlers. Acceptance is proven in the packaged harness (new section O, real actions on throwaway stores with real encryption): a December save stores enc:v1: ciphertext with no plaintext figures and reads back identical; a Roth UI-state save does the same; legacy plaintext rows planted directly in settings read back correctly; a backup carrying plaintext values for both keys restores to encrypted stored values that read back; and a stale-revision Roth UI-state write still conflicts. Verification repair (same build): the harness probe that reads the stored bytes first shipped calling the file's assertion helper where a database filter belonged (the helper shadows the database library's filter of the same name), so it read the first settings row instead of the probed key and the ciphertext assertions passed against the wrong row's bytes; the probe now selects all settings rows and finds the key, and the section passes against the correct row's bytes. The added text contains no first names and no hard-coded dollar figures. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 89 → 90.

## Net worth over time growth chart (build v68, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; client-only. Data rule: one point per snapshot from getNetWorth's already-loaded response, plotted from each snapshot's `totalCents` VERBATIM — that field is computed server-side by nwCore's `snapshotTotals` under exactly the view's own rules (custodial accounts never counted; property counted only while the "Include house & mortgage" toggle is on), and the component recomputes nothing, so the chart follows the toggle's current state automatically and can never disagree with the headline beside it. ## Result-honesty fixes & declutter (build v67, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; Half A settlement: ~/workspace/research_notes/chatgpt-result-honesty-audit-settlement-2026-10-27.md (five open SHOULD-FIXes built here: F04, F06, F07, F08, F09; F10/F11 stay logged nice-to-haves). The disease: readers converted an unreadable PRESENT record into the absent-record shape, so a damaged record priced as a fresh plan and a later save could silently replace it. The fix uses the codebase's own idiom — rothRevisionCore's {present:true, valid:false} state, which the strict Roth writer already refuses against. (F04) `updateMonthlyOneOff`'s editor in client/src/App.tsx now gates its onSuccess on the result like its four sibling editors: a refusal keeps the editor open with the edit intact and shows the reason. (F06) `readRetirementBlobState` reports revisionState {present, valid} (absent = {false, true}; unparseable or non-object = {true, false}); `getRetirementCalc` surfaces `savedUnreadable`; `saveRetirementCalc`, `saveRetirementBaseline`, and the scenario writers refuse against a present-but-invalid record and leave its bytes intact; the Retirement view renders a "Your saved record can't be read" alert instead of silently pricing the defaults as a fresh plan. (F07) `readRetirementBaselineState` was reshaped to always return {baseline, revision, storedRaw, present, valid} (readRetirementBaseline delegates to it); `getRetirementCalc` surfaces `baselineUnreadable` (and the session-baseline capture never runs against an unreadable baseline), `getRetirementBaselineResults` carries the same marker, and the Retirement view renders a matching baseline alert. (F08) `readRothBlob`'s unparseable and non-object branches now return revisionState {present:true, valid:false} with storedRaw retained (was {present:false, valid:true}); the existing `decideRothBlobWriteChecked` therefore refuses `saveRothInputs` against the corrupt state with NO writer change, and the raw readers (`readRothBlobRaw` / `readRothBlobRawState`) gained the same valid flag so the scenario writers and `resetRothPlanner` refuse too. `getRothPlanner` surfaces `recordUnreadable` (also on the writers' conflict records, via the one loadRothPlannerResponse), and the Tax Plan view renders the can't-be-read alert. (F09) December: the new `isDecemberStateUnparseable` in server/src/decemberCore.ts (present + JSON.parse throws / not a plain object; a parseable object with bad fields is still NOT unparseable and defaults leniently as before); `getDecemberProjection` returns `storedUnreadable`, the console renders the alert and names the unreadable case in its save-conflict note, and `saveDecemberProjection` refuses up front when the stored record is unparseable (conflict shape carrying storedUnreadable: true — an unparseable record is a conflict, never a revision-0 base; the other conflict returns carry storedUnreadable for their own after-state). Acceptance: packaged harness section N (N1–N34) plants each corruption honestly — a MAC-stripped export with one settings value replaced by unparseable text, restored through the real dispatcher — and proves getter marker present, writer refusal, and stored bytes intact per record, with absent-record and normal-record behaviour unchanged. Half B — the user's 2026-10-27 screenshot declutter picks: (1) Net Worth movers (client/src/YearBlocks.tsx TrendBlock): a Biggest gains / Biggest declines side with no entries is not rendered at all and the other side takes the full card width; both empty keeps the existing single neutral line. (3) More→ⓘ app-wide: the shared Explainer component (client/src/Explainer.tsx) now renders its summary line plus an ExplainerInfoTip carrying its full text word-for-word, and the More/Less fold + ExplainerToggle retired — converting, by that one component change, Spending: Slice & dice, the True-cost headline explainer, By category, Keep the lights on, Large one-offs, Monthly cash out, Coming up, Your data; Net Worth: Slice & dice, Accounts, History, Backups; Retirement: the view header (short line stays as the subtitle, the long mechanics text rides its ⓘ), Starting portfolio, Annual spending, Historical, Monte Carlo, Max Spending, Scenario compare. Hand-rolled More/Less explainers converted the same way: Tax Plan Work years and Gift stock (their persisted open-state fields remain in the UI-state blob shape, now unused), Playground's Projection methodology, and the Trend AnchorNote above. Kept visible, with reasons: the True-cost heads-up "Details/Less" toggle (its expanded text is a per-month computed reconciliation with live amounts inside a warning panel, not a static explainer); the optimizer's "How the search works" expander (a named methodology expander the v66 declutter deliberately left as the optimizer section's own control, not a More/Less link); the "Show the math"/"Hide the math" drill-downs in Tax Plan (they reveal priced per-year data tables, not explainer text). ## CAS sweep: stale-save refusal for every full-record editor (build v65, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; group B of the settled write-idempotency audit (settlement: ~/workspace/research_notes/chatgpt-write-idempotency-audit-settlement-2026-10-27.md; findings F11–F19, F22, F26, plus the F21 remainder). Goal: no full-record editor can silently overwrite a newer stored value with a stale form. Every refusal uses the established conflict shape ({ ok: false, conflict: true, reason } with the December-style "A newer copy was saved elsewhere" wording, built once in the new pure seam `server/src/casCore.ts` — casCanonical / casDeepEqual / casFieldMismatch / decideCasRevision / casConflictReason, pinned by the extended fixtures `api-cas-core-deep-equal` and `api-cas-core-field-mismatch-and-revision`), the stored newer value stays intact, and every live form now sends its loaded base, so no form-reachable hole remains. Mechanisms per family: (F11/F12) Net Worth snapshots gain a whole-snapshot revision counter — schema column `nw_snapshots.revision` (integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0) via migration 0026 (`ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN`, following the repo's additive-migration pattern; proven on a scratch database before shipping: a pre-0026-shaped table with rows migrates cleanly, existing rows read revision 0, new inserts default to 0, and a bump writes through) — returned by `getNetWorth` on every snapshot; `updateNwSnapshot` refuses when a supplied `baseRevision` differs from the stored revision and bumps it on an accepted write (inside the same atomic batch as the balance replacement), and `updateNwBalance` is folded into the same counter (refuses on a moved revision; bumps it on every accepted write, including a balance removal), so either editor's stale save conflicts instead of restoring old balances. Backup/restore does not carry the counter — the backup payload schema has no revision field, so a restored snapshot restarts at revision 0, exactly like a pre-v65 snapshot. (F13/F14) `updateTransaction` and `updateCashOutItem` are guarded updates: with a supplied `base` (the row's fields as loaded), the handler decrypt-compares the stored row against the base and then issues the UPDATE with a WHERE matching the id AND every raw stored column value it read, so the write applies only where the row still equals its loaded state even if a writer lands between the compare and the write; zero rows updated re-reads as conflict (row exists) or not-found (row gone). (F15) `upsertMonthlySummary` takes `base: { cashOutCents }` (null = no total was stored for the month) and refuses when the stored month total differs; its response widens from { ok: true } to the shared casOkResponse ({ ok, conflict?, reason? }). (F16) `setMonthlyBillAmount` takes `base: { amountCents }` (null = no version existed for that effective month) on top of v64's atomic upsert and refuses when the stored amount for (bill, effectiveFrom) differs. (F17) `updateYearlyExpense` takes a base of the parent fields (name, dueMonth, paidByType, paidByName, category, keepLightsOn) PLUS the version stored for the save's effective month (null = none); both halves are checked before ANY write, so a refusal leaves the parent and every version intact. (F18) `updateMonthlyBill` takes a base mirroring the bill's five form fields (schema in `server/src/apiContractCore.ts`); only the fields the save actually sends are compared. (F19) `renameNwAccount` takes a base of (name, propertyKind, custodial) and guards the fields the save writes (name always; propertyKind when sent or when custodial is being set; custodial when sent). (F22) `updateRothScenario` takes `baseScenario` (the named scenario's complete payload as loaded) and checks it INSIDE the existing blob CAS: the `mutateRothScenarios` transform refuses when the named scenario's stored payload no longer deep-equals the base, and because the check re-runs when the transform re-applies against a fresh blob, a concurrent write to a DIFFERENT scenario or to the working inputs does not refuse the save — blob freshness alone was never the guarantee, and now the scenario itself is guarded; the response gains `conflict: true` on this refusal. (F26) `updateSettings` takes a base of both keys (opening reserve, reserve start month) and refuses when either stored key differs, checked before either is written; its response likewise widens to casOkResponse. Client wiring: every in-scope editor sends its base — Spending (transaction, yearly expense incl. the history version at the chosen effective month, cash-out item, month summary incl. the import-panel proposal path which treats a refusal as a save failure, monthly bill + its chained amount save which no longer chains after a refused metadata save, reserve settings), Net Worth (snapshot editor and single-balance editor pass the snapshot's loaded revision; the rename row passes the account's loaded fields), and the Tax Plan strategy editor (the loaded scenario rides as baseScenario; a refusal keeps the editor open with the reason shown). Every guarded mutation's success handler now branches on the result: a refusal shows the reason in the form and does not reset or close it. (F21 remainder — verdict: a retry CAN complete, no code change) after a `saveRetirementBaseline` refusal the response carries the lite record with BOTH fresh revisions (and the client's applyConflictRecord already adopts them), so a retry using only those carried revisions finishes the baseline write; proven in packaged harness section M (M48–M54: inputs advanced past the baseline, a stale-base retry refused with record.revision 3 / baselineRevision 1 carried, the carried-revision retry completing with baseline == working inputs). A stage-"baseline" conflict itself requires two writers racing between the pair's two commits and cannot be forced sequentially through the public actions; the retry path it depends on is what section M exercises. TOLERATED MISSING-BASE PATHS (named per the brief): a crafted call that OMITS the base keeps the pre-v65 unchecked behaviour for updateTransaction, updateCashOutItem, updateYearlyExpense, updateMonthlyBill, setMonthlyBillAmount, upsertMonthlySummary, updateSettings, renameNwAccount, updateRothScenario (no baseScenario), and updateNwSnapshot / updateNwBalance (no baseRevision). This tolerance is deliberate and matches the codebase's existing posture — `saveRetirementCalc`, `saveRetirementBaseline`, and `setRothUiState` already accept an omitted baseRevision as a legacy path, while the strict writers (`saveRothInputs`, `saveDecemberProjection`) stay strict and unchanged. No live form omits the base after this build, so the tolerance is reachable only by a hand-crafted call, never by a stale screen. Acceptance: packaged harness section M exercises every family end-to-end through the real dispatcher (stale refused + stored newer value intact + fresh-base save succeeds per family, M1–M47) plus the F21 proof (M48–M54); the Net Worth snapshot editor and the Roth strategy editor surface the conflict reason in the form (their existing refusal rendering), satisfying the client-surfacing requirement alongside the harness evidence. API_CONTRACT_VERSION 64 → 65; the purpose text of every changed action was updated.

## Write-path structural fixes: uniqueness, first-write, atomic seed, migration guard, import keys (build v64, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; the 26 findings were confirmed from source at v60 (write-idempotency audit, settled 2026-10-27: 22 confirmed, 4 with nuance, 0 refuted). This build implements group A (A1–A4) plus the F02 import fix; group B (revision CAS for the full-record editors) is a later build (v65) and general request keys (group C) are logged, not built. (A1) Composite uniqueness + atomic upserts: migration 0025 adds plain `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` statements — `nw_balances_snapshot_account_unique` on nwBalances(snapshotId, accountId), `monthly_bill_versions_bill_effective_unique` on (billId, effectiveFrom), `yearly_expense_versions_expense_effective_unique` on (expenseId, effectiveFrom) — with matching `uniqueIndex` declarations in `server/src/schema.ts`. A plain unique index fails loudly on duplicates (no silent dedupe); proven on scratch databases before shipping: a clean scratch DB carrying migrations 0001–0024 and real-shaped data (same account in different snapshots, same bill/expense in different effective months) takes 0025 cleanly and then rejects duplicate-pair inserts, while a scratch DB seeded with duplicate pairs makes 0025 fail with a UNIQUE constraint error. `updateNwBalance`, `setMonthlyBillAmount`, `setYearlyExpenseVersion`, and `updateYearlyExpense`'s version write are now single atomic upserts on their pairs (`insert … onConflictDoUpdate`), so the read-then-insert races (F09 and the version-pair concern) cannot create a second row; no revision CAS was added to any of them (the stale-overwrite half is v65). (A2) Retirement first-write insert-if-absent (F20): `saveRetirementCalc` and `saveRetirementBaseline`, when the client supplies a base revision against a record that does not exist yet, write via insert `onConflictDoNothing` and return the existing conflict result shape when the insert did not land, mirroring `saveRothInputs`' first-write plan — two overlapping first saves at baseRevision 0 now produce exactly one success and one conflict instead of two revision-1 successes. Existing-record CAS behavior and the legacy no-base upserts are unchanged; `saveRetirementBaseline` keeps its stage reporting ("the working inputs were saved; the baseline did not move"), and F21's refused-retry nuance is accepted as the settlement describes it (no v65 CAS built to chase it). (A3) Atomic seeding + honest boot flag (F23, F24): `seedExamples`, `seedNetWorth`, and `seedFirstRun` now share batched statement builders (`seedExamplesStatements` / `seedNetWorthStatements`) that assign explicit row ids and return drizzle insert statements without executing them; each handler commits its statements as ONE `db.batch`, and `seedFirstRun` batches BOTH sets in a single batch, so a failure mid-seed leaves an empty dataset and a plain retry can succeed, and overlapping dispatches cannot double the roster (the loser sees the winner's rows at its emptiness check or its batch collides on the explicit ids / monthly-summary primary key and rolls back whole). The packaged boot caller (`packaged/src/runtime.ts`) sets `localDb.meta.seeded` ONLY when the seed result says `seeded: true` — a refusal (ok: true, seeded: false) leaves the flag unset so a later boot re-checks, instead of the pre-v64 behaviour of marking on ok alone and stranding a partial dataset. (A4) Legacy migration value-guard (F25 + the import-settings concern): every legacy-plaintext migration write — `loadAll`'s per-row re-encryptions (transactions incl. FITID, yearly expenses and their versions, monthly summaries, monthly bills incl. notes, monthly bill versions, one-offs, cash-out items, and the opening-reserve setting) and the import-settings getters' (`getImportData`, `getNwImportSettings`) settings rewrites — is now compare-and-write: the update's WHERE matches the row id AND every rewritten field's raw stored value as read, so a concurrent legitimate update wins over the migration rewrite; reads of already-encrypted data are byte-identical in behaviour. (F02) Import batch idempotency key: `importTransactions` accepts an optional `batchKey`; the completed key is recorded as a settings row (`import_batch_v1:<key>` → JSON {rows-hash, imported-count}) inserted inside the SAME `db.batch` as the transaction rows, so key and rows commit or roll back together. The settings-table home means the record survives in BOTH the hosted and packaged stores, rides the encrypted backup/restore settings array with the dataset it guards, and is wiped by clear-all-data alongside the rows. A retry with the same key and the same rows (matched by a SHA-256 hash of the canonical row tuples) returns the original `{ imported }` count and inserts zero rows; the same key with DIFFERENT rows is refused with a clear collision error and imports nothing; a new key with identical rows inserts (the key guards retries, not content); requests without a key behave exactly as before, and a batch refused by the existing import preflight records no claim. The client import panel (`client/src/App.tsx`) generates one key per batch attempt-set and reuses it when re-offering unacknowledged rows after a failure (the remaining rows are the same row objects; a fresh preview builds fresh objects and gets a fresh key). Group C (general request keys for the other append actions) and the Low append duplicates inside it (F01/F03–F08/F10 as a family) are logged, not built, per the settlement decision.

## Client-divergence fixes & packaged persist lockout (build v63, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; the four client findings and the packaged session hole were confirmed from source at v60 (client-divergence audit). (F1) Net Worth "Current buckets" (`client/src/NetWorth.tsx`): the headline and "% of target" now use the SIGNED sum of all bucket subtotals (`bucketSignedTotal`); the stacked mix bar stays positive-only (its denominator is the positive segments' sum), and any negative buckets render as their own lines under the bar so the displayed parts foot to the headline. With all buckets positive (the saved record's state) the sums are equal and the rendering is unchanged. (F4) Tax Plan Year Funding (`client/src/RothConversion.tsx`): `cashSpendCents` — the spend-from-cash sleeve share, one of the eleven funding sources that sum to each year's total need — is now rendered in both presentations whenever it is > 0: a "Cash sleeve used for spending" column in the years table (present when any priced year uses the sleeve) and a same-named row in the per-year "What funded it" breakdown (shown for that year when > 0), so listed sources foot to Total funded / total need. No engine change. (F2) Playground "Total tax" (`client/src/Playground.tsx`): the play strip's Total tax and the plain-English year line now show the engine's own `totalTax` (federal + state summed at cent precision) formatted at cent precision (`fmtDollarsExact`); the federal/state component figures are unchanged, and the sale-after-tax readout's deliberate component-first rounding (the engine's `saleAfterTax` and the strip's sale-leftover segment, which matches it) is untouched. (F3) Spending pre-start yearly-bill preview (`client/src/App.tsx`): a not-yet-in-effect bill's roster preview now takes amount, frequency, annualised figure, monthly set-aside, and start month all from the version in force at the start month (the earliest version — the history list's per-version `annualCents` / `monthlyAccrualCents`); when a later version first changes the amount or frequency, the preview names that change ("changes to … from …") as a note instead of pairing the latest amount with the earliest start. (F5) Packaged persist lockout (`packaged/src/runtime.ts`): a NON-STALE persist failure (quota, image verification — anything thrown after the handler mutated the in-memory image; the stale-tab refusal, which throws before any store write and is gated before any action runs, is excluded) now locks the session — the runtime records a reload-required reason (exposed as `sessionLocked` / `sessionLockReason`), the failed dispatch's 500 names the lock, and every further dispatch is refused with that error until reload, so the failed action's in-memory writes can never be silently committed by a later successful persist; the durable store's prior committed generation is untouched. Harness section I pins it: quota failure → lock engaged, subsequent read and write dispatches refused, a fresh load reads the prior generation intact with neither the failed nor the refused write present, and a stale-tab 409 does not engage the lock. December save-note fix (look-only item, demonstrated and fixed): in `client/src/December.tsx` a CAS conflict resolves as data (`ok: false`), and in @tanstack/query-core 5.100.10 the mutation-level `onSuccess` (which sets the "changed in another tab" note) is awaited inside `Mutation.execute` BEFORE the success dispatch notifies the per-call `mutate` callbacks — so the autosave's unguarded per-call `onSuccess: () => setSaveNote("Saved")` overwrote the conflict note in the same completion, and the still-dirty reloaded form would have cycled "Saving…" over it next. The per-call callback now says "Saved" only when `res.ok`, and the conflict branch clears the dirty flag before reloading the stored state into the form, so the conflict note survives until the user's next real edit. No server or engine behavior changes in this contract beyond the version stamp.

## December projection console (added Oct 2026)

Also user-entered only: year-to-date actuals, low / likely / high ranges for income still to come, ACA household / benchmark / advance-credit figures, and a strays checklist, saved as one settings blob (`december_projection_v1`) that rides the ordinary backup export / restore settings array. Pricing reuses the shipped single-year engine (`pricePlaygroundYear`) and its ACA-cliff solver (`solvePlaygroundAcaCliffFill`) from `server/src/rothOptimizer.ts` — no new tax math and no external source. On a first open the year block is preseeded from the saved Tax Plan record where available. Fixtures: the `december` suite of `runAccuracySelfCheck` (`runDecemberFixtures` in `server/src/decemberCore.ts`). December provenance (round-6, build v53): saves write a `decemberStateFormat` marker (now 3) — a pre-marker stored beneficiary `false` STANDS as a stored answer (the Tax Plan record overlay never overrides it) and parses with `legacyBeneficiaryAnswerUnconfirmed` set, so the console asks the user to confirm it and the flag clears only when the user changes that control; a with-marker `false` is likewise genuine; missing/null still reads unanswered. Load resolution from the Tax Plan record (beneficiary fact, legacy combined-balance ownership) is a display/pricing overlay that a save never persists for a field the user has not edited in the console (`decemberStateForSave`); a legacy combined balance with no split has ownership unanswered — when the record supplies both owner amounts with a positive sum, resolution allocates the SAVED combined total across the owners by the record split's proportions (the total itself never changes; a totals mismatch over $0.01 surfaces a console note naming both totals); when the record supplies exactly one owner amount, that owner receives min(known, saved total) and the other owner receives the remainder, both as numbers, so the total is still preserved exactly (the partial-cap case — exactly one amount known and above the saved total by more than $0.01 — likewise surfaces a console note naming the record figure and the saved total), combined→primary only as the last-resort fallback when the record has no usable split (neither amount known, or a both-known sum of $0), explicit blob split always governs; legacy stray amounts predating their tax-character splits (ROC capital/ordinary, January-paid qualified portion) carry unconfirmed-character flags that drive a view note and a projection warning and change no pricing — format-3 blobs carry the flags as stored (authoritative), pre-format-3 blobs derive them (split key absent or still at its default), and each flag clears ONLY when the user edits the matching character control, never on an unrelated save. Projected tax bill (build v50, reconciliation build v54): each priced case also carries readouts of the same priced year at the headline draw — adjusted gross income (AGI) (the year's AGI, labeled 'Adjusted gross income (AGI)' in the bill), taxable income, state tax, and a core-computed net settle. The ACA reconciliation prices in all years against the case's EFFECTIVE final credit: the priced credit when there is one; $0 when the priced credit is null because nobody in the household can be on the marketplace on the console's Medicare facts (a known-zero credit — the allowable credit is $0 by construction); null only when the priced credit is null AND someone is marketplace-eligible but no benchmark premium was entered (genuinely unpriced). creditAtHeadline itself stays the engine's priced credit, null in both null cases; only the reconciliation uses the effective value. creditStillDue is max(0, effective final credit − APTC taken) whenever the effective credit is known; excessAptcRepayment for 2026 and later is max(0, APTC taken − effective final credit) with no repayment caps, while before 2026 it is $0 when APTC taken is at or below the effective final credit and null when APTC taken exceeds it (repayment genuinely unmodeled — pre-2026 caps are not modeled), and null in every year when the credit is genuinely unpriced. The net settle (`totalTax − creditStillDue + excessAptcRepayment`) is nullable: null only when the repayment is unmodeled (pre-2026 APTC above the effective final credit) or the credit is genuinely unpriced, so a no-marketplace year still produces a number (the total tax, plus any repayment); each null net carries a reason note (`netSettleNote`) naming which case applies — the unpriced-credit reason wins whenever the credit itself is unpriced, in any year — and the note is null whenever the net is a number; a negative net is labeled 'Estimated refund at filing' and a non-negative net 'Estimated amount to settle at filing'; before withholding / estimated payments, which the console does not track — presented as a compact bill block for the likely case under the headline (income lines behind the block's own fold; tax / credit / net always visible) and as the net line on every case card. No new tax math: every figure is a readout of the existing `pricePlaygroundYear` pricing.

## Spending accounting corrections (build v59, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; settlement: ~/workspace/research_notes/chatgpt-spending-networth-audit-settlement-2026-10-27.md (all five audit findings confirmed). (F1) True cost now prices on ONE cash basis for every entry mode — cash out − settled yearly lumps + accrual — including transaction-only months, which previously priced on the incurred basis (card charges in their charge month). (F2) The yearly-payment correction follows the money: card payments are matched FIFO against outstanding card-paid yearly charges, so the correction fires in the settlement month (the month money leaves checking), and `yearlyPaidOutCents` counts a yearly payment in its settlement month; a household that records only the payout (a checking transaction in the payout month, never the charge) prices bit-identically to before. (F3) Smoothed-bill set-asides use cumulative rounding per bill — month n accrues round(annual × n/12) − round(annual × (n−1)/12) — so each bill's twelve monthly set-asides sum to its annual amount exactly; every consumer (bill cards, Keep-the-lights-on floor, dashboard, Explorer, Year Summary) reads the one function (`monthlyAccrualForAnnual` in `server/src/spendingCore.ts`). (F4) `getDashboard`'s trailing averages never include months after the current calendar month, whatever month is selected, and history rows for months after the current month carry `estimate: true`. (F5) The Explorer's True-cost residual row (bill/category groupings) is now labeled "Other spending", distinct from the Month grouping's cash-out plug, which keeps the label "Everything else"; the Year Summary's top-categories residual uses the same "Other spending" label. Acceptance pinned in the extended fixtures: `sp-cash-basis-micro-case` (Jan/Feb/Mar True cost $1,100 / $1,400 / $1,100), `sp-card-settlement-attribution` (February prices $100, not $1,300), `sp-accrual-cumulative-conservation` (a $100/yr bill's twelve set-asides sum to exactly $100.00).

## Statute-fixed deflation sweep & citation corrections (build v61, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; settlement: ~/workspace/research_notes/chatgpt-law-table-audit-settlement-2026-10-27.md (all four audit findings confirmed; every published 2025/2026 nominal value verified correct against its authority — the defects were classification/consumption, not table values). The engine's standing rule — statute-fixed (non-indexed) dollar amounts deflate by `deflationFactor(calendarYear, law.year, inflationPct)` in today's-dollars projections while indexed amounts stay flat, factor 1.0 for a year with its own law row — now reaches the four amounts that escaped it. (F1) Washington's $1,000,000 capital-gains surtax threshold (RCW 82.87.040(1)(b), absent from RCW 82.87.150's indexed list): `priceYear` threads its `defl` into `waCapitalGainsTax` (new optional factor argument, default 1, so direct fixture calls pin current-year behavior bit-identically) and only the threshold is scaled; the DOR-indexed WA standard deduction and charitable threshold/cap stay nominal. The published STATE_SEMANTICS text is rewritten to the settled rule (it previously stated the threshold does NOT deflate) and its extended-fixture phrase pin re-pinned. Acceptance: 2027 off the 2026 row at 3% inflation, $1,000,000 of taxable WA gains → deflated threshold $970,873.79, tax $70,844.66 (was $70,000). (F2) The §3101(b)(2) Additional Medicare threshold in work years: `priceOneWorkYear` computes the year's factor from `plan.inflationPct` and threads it into `payrollTaxBreakdown` / `ficaTax` (optional factor, default 1). Acceptance: MFJ FICA wages $260,000 priced as 2027 off the 2026 row at 3% → Additional Medicare Tax $155.53 (was $90.00). (F3) The §223(b)(3) HSA age-55 catch-up ($1,000, fixed since 2009) deflates by the same threaded factor inside `contributionStack`; the indexed base limits stay as read. Acceptance: 55-year-old, family coverage, 2027 off the 2026 row at 3% → limit $8,750 + $970.87 = $9,720.87 (was $9,750). (F4) The §170(p) non-itemizer charitable cap deflates by `defl` at its use site in `priceYear`, mirroring the senior deduction in the same function. Acceptance: MFJ, $100,000 AGI, $2,000 qualifying giving, standard deduction taken, priced as 2027 at 3% → cap $1,941.75, taxable income $65,858.25, federal tax $7,406.99 ($6.99 above the undeflated pricing). Each acceptance case is pinned as a `v61-*` fixture in `server/src/taxFixtures.ts` with its derivation. CITATION CORRECTIONS (wording only, no numeric change): the OBBBA senior deduction is IRC §151(d)(5)(C) (P.L. 119-21 §70103), NOT §224 (§224 is the qualified-tips deduction) — 65 occurrences of "§224" naming the senior deduction corrected across `server/src/taxLaw.ts` (3), `server/src/taxEngine.ts` (23), `server/src/decemberCore.ts` (1), `server/src/apiContractCore.ts` (5), `server/src/taxFixtures.ts` (26), and this file (7); the §56(b)(5)(D) AMT add-back citations are a different, correct authority and are untouched. And `server/src/taxLaw.ts` now cites Rev. Proc. 2024-25 (not 2024-18) for the 2025 HSA limits; values unchanged.

## Packaged build & backup integrity (build v60, 2026-10-27)

All user-entered data, no external source; settlement: ~/workspace/research_notes/chatgpt-packaged-parity-audit-settlement-2026-10-27.md (all nine audit findings confirmed). (F1–F3) The packaged browser store (`packaged/src/localDb.ts`) is redesigned around immutable generation-stamped images under a single active-generation pointer (`fpkg:v1:active` = {gen, chunks, sha256}): a persist writes the new generation's chunks, verifies them by SHA-256 and by opening the bytes, and only then switches the pointer, retaining the previous generation; a corrupt/incomplete/checksum-failing active image refuses boot with a recovery-required error and writes nothing (a genuinely fresh store still initializes empty); pre-v60 in-place chunk stores are adopted once and re-persisted as generation 1. The migration count lives inside the image (`PRAGMA user_version`, stamped from the legacy meta only for that one adoption) and commits atomically with the schema. Stale-tab protection: a tab persists — and dispatches at all — only while the store's active generation is the one it loaded or last wrote; a mismatch is refused with a reload instruction (dispatch 409), including for read-only actions. (F4) Restore preflight now enforces every backed-up field's writer rule through shared zod fragments (`server/src/fieldValidators.ts`, imported by both the writer schemas in actions.ts and the backup schemas in restoreCore.ts): string lengths, dueMonth 1–12, 0/1 flag representations, positive ids/foreign keys, and no tax-bucket split on property/custodial balances; named exclusions are published in the restorebackup contract text (opaque settings blobs other than the three scalar typed settings, the legacy NW `bucket` column, server-assigned sortOrder/createdAt). The extended fixture `restore-writer-illegal-fields-refused-preflight` mutates every backed-up field to a writer-illegal value and requires refusal before any write. The sweep also caught — via the F5 cross-install acceptance — two encrypted-at-rest settings (`entry_default_monthly_paid_from_v1`, `entry_default_yearly_paid_name_v1`) missing from both the export decrypt list and restoreCore's `ENCRYPTED_AT_REST_SETTING_KEYS`; both lists now carry them, and the key-list fixture is re-pinned at nine keys. (F5) Portable encrypted backups for the packaged build (`packaged/src/portableBackup.ts` + a panel in `packaged/src/main.tsx`): export downloads a `.mstbak` envelope (format `mst-backup-portable` v1, PBKDF2-SHA256 210k iterations → AES-256-GCM) of the exportbackup payload under a user-chosen passphrase — the passphrase is the only key and is never stored; import decrypts and runs the existing validated restorebackup. Harness-proven install A → fresh install B end to end. The live build's backup behavior (server key, Backups panel, weekly job) is unchanged. (F6) Plan-year capture in the Roth compute paths is UTC: runRothOptimizer, runRothCompare, runRothMonteCarloCheck, runRothMonteCarloStats, runWorkYearsCompare, and the December console's parse-year sites (getDecemberProjection / saveDecemberProjection) use `getUTCFullYear()`; dashboard month strings, effectiveFrom defaults, seed windows, the Retirement default age, and the non-listed Roth readers (runRothGiftCompare, runPlanYearDetail, runRothFunding, computeEffectiveInputs' legacy fallback) deliberately stay on the local clock. (F7) One global first-run emptiness predicate (`server/src/seedGuardCore.ts`) over all twelve dataset tables (settings presence excludes only the encryption key-check row), failing closed on unreported tables; both seed actions use it, the new `seedFirstRun` action runs it once and seeds both datasets as one operation, and the packaged runtime marks the store seeded only from that action's result. (F8) `.github/workflows/pages.yml` runs `bun run harness` (fixture census included) as a hard gate before the deploy steps. (F9) The packaged probe's Playground goldens are corrected to MAGI $121,500 / federal tax $8,360, matching the harness.

## Retirement calculator — historical dataset (build-time, embedded)

Embedded in `client/src/retirementData.ts` (annual, 1928–2025):

- Stocks (S&P 500 total return incl. dividends) and bonds (US 10-year Treasury total return): Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern — Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills, updated Jan 5, 2026.
  Source URL (verbatim): https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histretSP.html
  Spot checks against the source page: 2008 stocks −36.55%; 2022 stocks −18.04% and bonds −17.83% (both negative) — all match.
- Inflation (CPI-U annual average percent change): U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI-U (public-domain BLS series), as published in BLS CPI tables and mirrored at https://cpiinflationcalculator.com/historical-tables/ (retrieved Oct 2026). Annual-average rates used (e.g. 2008 3.8%, 2022 8.0%).

The calculator converts nominal to real returns as (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) − 1, blends by the user's stock/bond mix, and replays every historical start year with a full plan-length sequence. The source name and URL are cited in a footnote on the calculator screen.

- Full dataset audit (2026-10-11): all 98 years × 3 series (294 values) in the embedded dataset (now at `server/src/retirementData.ts`, shared by the client view and the server) were compared programmatically against the published sources — stocks/bonds vs Damodaran's table as updated Jan 5, 2026 (URL above; the published page's data table mirrors the histretSP spreadsheet, whose direct .xls link returned 404 to the fetcher), CPI vs the BLS CPI-U annual-average percent changes as published in the BLS CPI-U table (monthly values and Avg–Avg percent changes, mirrored at https://www.coinnews.net/tools/cpi-inflation-calculator/consumer-price-index-cpi-and-annual-percent-changes-from-1913-to-2008/ and cross-checked against the BLS percent-change table at https://files.snappages.site/j4hr5rfob1/assets/files/Inflation.pdf). Result: 0 discrepancies at rounding tolerance (|diff| ≤ 0.011); no values changed.

Published comparison: Cooley, Hubbard & Walz (1998), the Trinity Study, Table 3 (inflation-adjusted, 30-year, 4%): 50/50 = 95%, 75/25 = 100% (1926–1995 Ibbotson data, corporate bonds) — as analysed at https://retirementresearcher.com/safe-withdrawal-rates-for-retirement-and-the-trinity-study/ and summarised at https://keepthrifty.com/ (search-surfaced summary).
